newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Asian copper steady, supply problems to cap losses.
newsitem.headline: Asian copper steady, supply problems to cap losses.

text.p: London Metal Exchange (LME) three-month copper prices were barely changed in thin Asian trade on Wednesday, but jitters over supply problems were seen limiting further losses, Far Eastern traders said.
"Copper prices are expected to consolidate at around US$2,350 a tonne in the very short term," a trader with LG Futures said.
Three-month copper was traded at $2,363 a tonne at 0500 GMT, up marginally from Tuesday's LME close of $2,362.
The benchmark cash-to-three months backwardation was at $75/$80 on Tuesday, down from a high of $90 but off the low of $60/$65.
LME broker Macquarie said in its daily report the copper market remained extremely tight despite the drop in cash prices this week.

Macquarie said the strike in northern Chile's Escondida mine and a decision by workers at the Quebrada Blanca mine on the Chilean-Bolivian border to go on strike later on Wednesday weighed on the market.
A drought in central and southern Chile, which may pinch power supplies for copper mines in the country, is also a cause for concern, the report added.
"Rationing has already been introduced for domestic power users in Santiago. The next step would be restrictions on industrial users," Macquarie said.

"If there is no substantial rainfall within the next two to four weeks, power supplies could be cut off for one day per week. Chile is just entering its rainy season. However, latest weather forecasts showed some cloud, but little rain," it said.

The main mines around Santiago which could be affected are La Candelaria, with an annual capacity of 140,000 tonnes, El Teniente, with a capacity of 340,000 tonnes, Andina mine and El Soldado among others, it said.
The four mines account for around 7.5 percent of Western copper production.
Smelters at El Teniente Las Vantanas and Disputada were also expected to be affected by any power rationing.
Meanwhile, traders said aluminium prices on the Tokyo Commodity Exchange (TOCOM) rose on Wednesday on the back of firmer prices in London.
TOCOM's benchmark February aluminium contract rose to 211.7 yen per kg at 0600 GMT, up 1.7 yen from Tuesday's close.
"There was some persistent hedge buying from trading houses and short-covering from speculators in dull trading," a trader at Japanese broker Okachi and Co Ltd said.
But LME broker Brandeis said in its daily report that the upside looked rather limited with good resistance at $1,640 and then $1,650 a tonne.
A move back to close the gap between $1,620 and $1,614 seemed more likely, unless good levels of consumer buying were seen at these level, it said.
A trader with LG Futures said LME copper and aluminium stocks were expected to continue falling on Wednesday. He did not estimate the size of the decline.
